Macroeconomic Forecasting & Inflation Surge Detection

A multi-indicator machine learning and time-series framework for semiconductor and other electronic component manufacturing PPI, using FRED data.

01 · Research problem

Why forecast semiconductor-sector inflation?

Producer prices in semiconductor and electronic component manufacturing may respond to input costs, production conditions and sector-specific market changes. The project tests whether a combination of historical inflation and macroeconomic indicators can provide useful forecasts and early warning signals.

Forecasting challenge

Monthly PPI contains trend, seasonality, changing regimes and occasional extreme movements. A model that performs well in stable periods may fail during abrupt changes.

Indicator challenge

Commodity prices and manufacturing indicators may add information, but their predictive value must be demonstrated through chronological evaluation.

Research question

Can a regime-aware, multi-indicator framework improve six-month-ahead PPI forecasting and identify unusually strong inflation momentum?

03 · External evidence investigation

What happened around January–February 2026?

The notebook identified an unusually sharp movement in the semiconductor/electronic-component PPI. We investigated BLS detailed industry tables to determine whether the broad industry movement was uniform across sub-industries.

BLS industry 3344

Printed circuit assembly 334418
+43.5%
Index 99.132 → 142.274
Semiconductor device mfg 334413
+2.3%
Index 29.566 → 30.234
Key interpretation: The BLS detailed table indicates that the sharp broad-industry movement was not uniform. Printed circuit assembly (334418) showed a much larger monthly index increase than semiconductor and related device manufacturing (334413). This is consistent with a concentrated sub-industry movement, but it does not by itself prove the economic cause or quantify each industry's weighted contribution to the aggregate index.

Open BLS March 2026 PPI Detailed Report ↗

Why this matters for our model

Our target series aggregates a sector with potentially different sub-industry price dynamics. A sudden change in one component can create a structural break for a model trained on the earlier aggregate history. The correct research conclusion is that the model faced a sharp regime change; attributing the change to a single cause requires further weighted industry-level evidence.

"We noticed a sudden increase in our target around early 2026. Instead of treating the movement as a normal fluctuation, we checked the BLS detailed PPI report. The broad 3344 industry rose 9.2% from January to February. Within the detailed industries, printed circuit assembly rose much more sharply, while semiconductor device manufacturing rose by a smaller amount. This suggests that the aggregate movement may reflect different behaviour across sub-industries. It is an important structural-change clue, not proof of a single cause."

04 · Methodology

From economic indicators to forecasts

Target transformation

Year-over-year PPI inflation is calculated from the PPI index level:

πₜ = 100 × (PPIₜ / PPIₜ₋₁₂ − 1)

The model predicts the inflation rate, not the raw index level.

Direct multi-horizon targets

Six supervised targets are built:

Target Hₕ(t) = πₜ₊ₕ, h = 1,…,6

Each horizon has a separate model and a forecast based on information at origin t.

Model families tested

Baselines & ML

Persistence, Ridge Regression, Random Forest and XGBoost.

Statistical models

ARIMA, seasonal ARIMA and SARIMAX with exogenous manufacturing/commodity indicators.

Regime adaptation

Expanding windows compared with rolling 120- and 180-month estimation windows.

Chronological evaluation design

Direct-horizon experiment: training origins July 1993–December 2016 (282 observations), validation July 2017–December 2019 (30 observations), followed by later development observations. A six-month separation was used to reduce overlap/leakage between target windows.

Earlier statistical six-month-ahead experiment: 73 evaluation forecasts over the reported 2019–2026 period. This is a separate experiment and its metrics must not be mixed with the direct H1–H6 validation results.

What do MAE, RMSE and R² mean?

MAE is the average absolute forecast error; RMSE penalizes larger errors more heavily; R² compares model error with a mean benchmark and can be negative. Here, MAE and RMSE are measured in percentage points of YoY PPI inflation.

SARIMAX forecast evaluation

Historical actual-versus-predicted comparison from the notebook.

Feature importance (model-specific)

Feature importance describes a fitted model’s reliance on features; it is not a causal ranking.
The statistical SARIMAX results and the direct H1–H6 machine-learning results use different target constructions and evaluation windows. Treat them as complementary experiments, not a head-to-head leaderboard.

Residual diagnostics and uncertainty

Residual diagnostics

Residuals were strongly non-normal/heavy-tailed; Ljung–Box tests did not detect significant autocorrelation at tested lags 12 and 24.

Prediction interval calibration

Recent empirical coverage deteriorated, indicating historical residual calibration did not capture the latest regime.
How to explain the best statistical model

"The rolling 180-month SARIMAX achieved an MAE of 1.6989 across 73 six-month-ahead evaluation observations. The rolling window can adapt more quickly than an expanding window because older observations gradually leave the estimation sample. However, the model still struggled to anticipate the initial 2026 inflation surge."

06 · Inflation surge detection

Defining a surge objectively

Ten momentum and volatility features were engineered: 1-, 3- and 6-month inflation momentum; 1- and 3-month acceleration; rolling means; rolling volatility; consecutive increases; and a historical momentum Z-score.

Training period
1993–2016
Chronological training data
Surge threshold
2.3223
95th percentile, positive 3M momentum
Surge months
15
Historical flagged months
Event frequency
3.82%
15 of 393 observations
Surge definition: Mₜ(3) = πₜ − πₜ₋₃. A surge is flagged when Mₜ(3) exceeds 2.3223 percentage points, a threshold calculated using positive momentum observations in the training period only.

Latest surge behaviour in the notebook

The momentum method identifies sharp upward acceleration, not necessarily positive inflation. Historical 2004 and 2008 detections occurred while YoY inflation was negative.

Detected months include August–October 2004; February–May and October 2008; October–November 2021; August–October 2025; and February–March 2026. Consecutive months may be part of one surge episode rather than separate independent events.

Prospective warning labels: positive event counts

07 · Final direct forecast

Six separate monthly PPI inflation forecasts

The final integrated run uses the September 2026 forecast origin. The selected model differs by horizon, based on validation MAE.

Final H1–H6 forecast and empirical 95% ranges

Uploaded final forecast plot. The six orange points are separate direct-horizon forecasts.
MonthHorizonModelForecast YoY95% lower95% upperValidation MAE
H4 caveat: January 2027 uses the persistence model and carries forward the latest observed inflation value (26.0152%). It is not an independently estimated trend. Forecasts are separate horizon predictions, not a smooth recursive path.
Prediction intervals: The 80% and 95% bands are empirical ranges based on validation absolute errors. Because the series experienced structural change and recent undercoverage, they are not guaranteed coverage intervals.

"This is the main operational output. We generate one prediction for each month from October 2026 to March 2027. Each horizon has its own selected model. The shaded area shows empirical validation-error ranges. The forecast suggests elevated sector PPI inflation across this forecast window, but the model-selection and interval limitations should be kept in mind."

Illustrative smartphone scenario

Scenario assumes ₹30,000 base price, 50% pass-through and assumed 24% BOM share coverage.

What this scenario means

The model combines forecast commodity movements and derived semiconductor PPI index changes using assumed BOM shares. It applies an assumed 50% pass-through rate to produce an illustrative price adjustment.

This is not a validated smartphone retail-price forecast. BOM shares are assumptions, and sector PPI is not the actual purchase price of a specific handset manufacturer.

10 · Limitations & conclusion

What the project demonstrates—and what it does not

What we demonstrated

  • Integrated six-indicator monthly FRED dataset.
  • Chronological comparison of baseline, ML and statistical models.
  • Evidence that rolling 180-month SARIMAX improved the reported six-month-ahead statistical benchmark.
  • Direct H1–H6 forecast generation with horizon-specific models.
  • Historical inflation surge definition and warning outputs.
  • Reusable CSV outputs and research visualizations.

Important limitations

  • Sharp structural changes are difficult to forecast from earlier regimes.
  • Residuals are heavy-tailed and non-normal.
  • Recent prediction interval coverage is poor.
  • Surge labels are rare; early-warning classifier performance is not yet established.
  • Historical periods were repeatedly used during model development.
  • Phone-price scenario uses assumed BOM shares and pass-through.
  • Real-time use requires data-release timing and vintage controls.
Conclusion

The project builds an integrated framework for semiconductor-sector PPI analysis, statistical and machine-learning forecasting, and inflation-momentum monitoring. The experiments show that model choice and estimation window matter, but abrupt structural changes remain a major forecasting challenge. The BLS sub-industry evidence provides a useful lead for investigating the 2026 movement without claiming an unsupported single cause.
